conventions.convention: Pell's equation uses a positive nonsquare integer D; a positive nontrivial solution has x>0 and y>0, excluding (±1,0).
Generalized Pell equations on this page require N≠0; the zero-norm equation is outside scope.
The arithmetic is performed in the explicit order Z[√D]={x+y√D:x,y∈Z}, with conjugate x−y√D and norm N_D(x+y√D)=x²−Dy²; this is not asserted to be the full ring of integers.
Convergents are indexed from n=0 using p_{−2}=0, p_{−1}=1, q_{−2}=1, q_{−1}=0.
For the square-root state convention P₀=0 and Q₀=1, the norm identity has sign p_n²−Dq_n²=(−1)^{n+1}Q_{n+1}.
The fundamental Pell solution minimizes the first coordinate among solutions with x,y>0, and ε_D denotes x₁+y₁√D>1.
Pell-equivalence means multiplication by ε_D^k for k∈Z, without an additional sign; consequently α and −α can represent different orbits.
An unqualified Artinian ring is unital and left Artinian; every owned ring theorem then explicitly restricts to the commutative case.
A local ring is nonzero and has exactly one maximal ideal.
The Artinian-to-Noetherian and downstream length, local-decomposition, prime-characterisation, and localization statements explicitly assume the Axiom of Choice.
The zero module has the empty composition series and length 0.
The Chinese remainder theorem is stated for a nonempty finite family I₁,…,I_r with r≥1.
The zero ring is handled separately as having no maximal ideals; the canonical product-of-localizations assertion is stated for nonzero Artinian rings.

load_bearing.statement: Let D be a positive integer that is not a square and a₀=⌊√D⌋. Then there is an integer ℓ≥1 such that √D=[a₀; overline(a₁,…,a_{ℓ−1},2a₀)], with a_j=a_{ℓ−j} for 1≤j<ℓ. The first returned reduced state is P_ℓ=a₀, Q_ℓ=1.
Let R be a commutative Artinian ring and let p be a prime ideal of R. Then p is maximal.
Let R be a commutative Artinian ring. Then the nilradical Nil(R) is a nilpotent ideal. This theorem uses dependent choice only through the minimum condition for Artinian modules.
For pairwise comaximal ideals I₁,…,I_r with r≥1, the canonical map R→∏R/I_i is surjective, has kernel ∩I_i, and ∩I_i=∏I_i; equivalently R/∏I_i≅∏R/I_i.
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let R be a commutative Artinian ring. Then R is Noetherian.

The negative Pell equation x²−Dy²=−1 has an integral solution if and only if the continued-fraction period length ℓ is odd. For odd ℓ, p_{ℓ−1}/q_{ℓ−1} is the least positive negative-Pell solution and p_{2ℓ−1}/q_{2ℓ−1} is the least positive norm-one solution; for even ℓ, p_{ℓ−1}/q_{ℓ−1} is the least positive norm-one solution.

Every integral solution x²−Dy²=N, with D positive nonsquare and N≠0, is Pell-equivalent to x₀+y₀√D satisfying |x₀|≤(√|N|/2)(√ε_D+ε_D^{−1/2}) and |y₀|≤(√|N|/(2√D))(√ε_D+ε_D^{−1/2}); consequently there are only finitely many Pell-equivalence classes.
Every positive integral solution of x²−Dy²=1 is equal to ε_D^k for a unique integer k≥1.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If a commutative Artinian ring R is nonzero with maximal ideals m₁,…,m_r, then the canonical map R→∏R_{m_i} is an isomorphism. If Nil(R)^n=0, then also R≅∏R/m_i^n; the localization product is canonical, while the quotient-by-powers form depends on n.

concerns.concern: Step 2.1 calls S finite, but its displayed definition does not impose the earlier bound |P|<√D. For D=2, every m≥3 gives (P,Q)=(-m,m²-2) in that S, so the finite-cycle argument needs the missing restriction and the corresponding inverse-map check.
Step 1.2 infers D-P_{n+1}²>0 from only P_{n+1}<√D. A lower bound P_{n+1}>-√D is also needed; it can be derived using the complete-quotient inequalities, but is not written.

Step 2.1 obtains the stated bound on β+|conjugate(α₀)| by merely listing separate upper bounds β,|conjugate(α₀)|≤√|N|√ε_D, which only yields 2√|N|√ε_D. The sharper √|N|(√ε_D+ε_D^{-1/2}) bound needs the endpoint/convexity argument for t+1/t; the claimed strict lower bound for the conjugate can also be equality.

Step 3.1 says convergent denominators strictly increase, but q₀=q₁=1 can occur, as for √3. Leastness remains recoverable by using strict increase from q₁ onward and checking the relevant candidate indices, but the stated justification is false as written.

Steps 2.1 and 3.1 infer p_{ℓ-1}>0 from an equation for p_{ℓ-1}². Positivity follows from the convergent recurrence and positive digits, not from that square equation alone, and the needed derivation is absent.
Nonemptiness of the positive-solution set does not by itself produce an element with least first coordinate; well-ordering of its positive integer x-coordinates is the missing well-definedness step.
The statement permits r=1, but surjectivity and the kernel computation are proved only for r≥2. The r=1 case is the canonical quotient map and is immediate, but it is not supplied.

The proof immediately treats Nil(R) and all its powers as ideals. The cited nilradical definition identifies its elements but the local proof does not cite or derive the standard fact that a radical is an ideal.

Step 1.1 identifies Nil(R) with the intersection of the listed maximal ideals using only that every prime is maximal. The converse inclusion of index sets requires the standard fact that every maximal ideal of a commutative ring is prime, which is neither cited nor derived here.
Step 1.1 shows that every prime, if present, must equal the unique maximal ideal, but it also needs to establish that the maximal ideal is prime before concluding it is the only prime and Nil(R)=m.
The equality Nil(R)=m₁∩⋯∩m_r again uses only prime-implies-maximal; it also needs maximal-implies-prime. That uncited standard fact underlies the subsequent CRT decomposition.

Step 1.2 uses that every prime ideal contains a minimal prime over (0), whereas the cited theorem as opened only states finiteness of minimal primes. The containment/existence fact needs a citation or short derivation.

After decomposing R into local factors, step 2.1 continues to write S∩m and S^{-1}A without defining the image of the original multiplicative set in each factor. Interpreting S as its projected image closes the argument, but the expressions are not literally well-formed as written.

The finite rectangle depends on ε_D, but the proof does not explicitly explain how ε_D is computed from the fixed input D. The preceding continued-fraction construction or an enumerative search plus Pell existence supplies the terminating procedure, but that algorithmic link should be stated for a decidability claim.

Step 1.1 ranges over all k∈Z without explicitly establishing that ε_D^k remains in Z[√D] for negative k. Since ε_D^{-1} is its integral conjugate, this is immediate, but the group/inverse step is omitted.

The verification proves that 15/4 is the first displayed convergent with norm 1, but the cited period structure and norm identity alone do not show it is the least positive Pell solution. A citation to the parity/leastness theorem or the finite check y=1,2,3 is needed.
Step 3.1 says to take m=i-1 in step 2.1, whose range is 1≤m<i. This is invalid when i=1; that boundary case is already proved in step 1.1 and only needs to be split off.
